newsitem.title: USA: Bumpy start for US power transmission data system.
newsitem.headline: Bumpy start for US power transmission data system.

text.p: Technical problems marred the debut Friday of the U.S. electricity industry's Open Access Same-time Information System (OASIS), according to traders using the government-mandated system.

OASIS, put in place by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, is part of the commission's efforts to widen access to power transmission capacity to include marketers and others who do not own power lines.
The Internet-based system contains information for real-time prices as well as transmission capacity.
"Everything is still being done by fax," said a power marketer who deals in the Electricity Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT).
"It's not fully operational. They have a lot of problems. They can't even get access to it," the ERCOT marketer said.
A trading manager at a California utility said access to the system came and went throughout the day.
But some of the headaches were blamed on staff not knowing the right password or similar user errors.
"We don't really know how much is our physical problem and how much is OASIS," the California trading manager noted.
"For the transmission I needed, it was pretty inoperable," a New York electricity trader said, adding transmission tariffs and available capacity for many utilities were not posted online.
"A lot of providers didn't have them in on time because the systems were up and down, up and down," he said.
A utility trader in New Mexico said "this is not only a change in the system, it is a total change in culture. Some oldtimers are resisting it."
He noted the electricity industry is "very relationship intensive, people want to dicker over the phone."
Under the FERC requirements, traders cannot talk directly to transmission operators in their own company.
Nevertheless, market sources said they expect using the system to get easier as more people become familiar with it.
